h1: The 6 Best Wi-Fi Extenders of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 Wi-Fi extenders compared on Wi-Fi standard, 5 GHz speed, antenna design and Ethernet ports, from AX3000 to budget AC1200 units.
summary: The TP-Link AX3000 is the best Wi-Fi extender: Wi-Fi 6, up to 2404 Mbps on 5 GHz, and directional antennas with beamforming. The TP-Link RE550 AC1900 is the best value for a mid-size home, covering up to 2,100 sq ft with three adjustable antennas. For the smallest budget, the TP-Link RE315 does the job under $25. Avoid trusting the 5,200 sq ft claim on the PEDUMMY.
intro: An extender does not add speed; it repeats a signal, and every repeat costs bandwidth. A single-radio extender talking to the router and your phone on the same channel can halve throughput, which is why the cheapest units often disappoint on streaming. The spec that matters most is not the headline coverage number but whether the extender has a separate 5 GHz link back to the router.

That is the lens for this ranking of six extenders, from an AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 unit to a $25 AC1200. We reviewed each spec sheet and compared bandwidth, antenna design, Ethernet ports and the plausibility of coverage claims. Where a listing's claim looks inflated, as with a 5,200 sq ft promise on a 1200 Mbps unit, we say so and rank accordingly.

products.name: TP-Link AX3000 WiFi 6 Dual-Band Range Extender
products.verdict: Wi-Fi 6 with up to 2404 Mbps on 5 GHz and directional antennas with beamforming.
products.description:
The AX3000 is a Wi-Fi 6 dual-band extender with 3 Gbps total bandwidth, up to 2404 Mbps on 5 GHz, coverage of up to 2,400 sq ft and two high-gain directional antennas with beamforming. It is the only Wi-Fi 6 unit in this group.

It wins because the 5 GHz figure is more than double the AC1900's, which matters when the link back to your router is the bottleneck. Beamforming aims the signal at devices instead of broadcasting evenly. The cost is price: it sits in the $100 to $200 bracket, far above the others.

Buy it with a Wi-Fi 6 router, where it can use its full speed. With an older router, the extra bandwidth sits idle.
products.idealFor: Homes with a Wi-Fi 6 router and dead zones.
products.skipIf: Your router is Wi-Fi 5 or you are on a tight budget.

products.name: TP-Link AC1900 WiFi Range Extender RE550
products.verdict: AC1900 with three adjustable antennas covering up to 2,100 sq ft.
products.description:
The RE550 is a Wi-Fi 5 AC1900 dual-band extender with 1.9 Gbps total bandwidth, up to 2,100 sq ft of coverage and three adjustable external antennas. Expect to pay $25 to $50.

Second place follows since it delivers almost the AX3000's coverage for a fraction of the price, and because adjustable antennas let you angle signal along a hallway or up a stairwell. It trails the leader in raw 5 GHz speed and loses Wi-Fi 6 features, which only matter on a newer router.

Buy it for a mid-size house with an AC router. The listing does not state a separate 5 GHz backhaul, so expect some throughput loss when two devices share the link.
products.idealFor: Mid-size homes with a Wi-Fi 5 router.

products.name: TP-Link AC1200 WiFi Extender RE315
products.verdict: 867 Mbps on 5 GHz, two external antennas and Adaptive Path Selection for under $25.
products.description:
The RE315 is an AC1200 dual-band extender with 867 Mbps on 5 GHz, up to 1,500 sq ft of coverage, two adjustable external antennas and Adaptive Path Selection, which picks the best route back to the router. It is the cheapest TP-Link here.

It ranks third because its 1,500 sq ft figure is lower than the RE550's 2,100 sq ft, and it has no Ethernet port. What it offers is a stated 5 GHz speed at the lowest brand price, and a path-selection feature that other budget units skip.

Buy it for an apartment or a single dead bedroom. The caveat is that coverage figures assume open space, so walls cut real reach.
products.skipIf: You need a wired port or a big coverage area.

products.name: NETGEAR WiFi Extender EX5000
products.verdict: AC1200 with setup through the Nighthawk app or a WPS button.
products.description:
NETGEAR's EX5000 is an AC1200 Wi-Fi 5 extender with 1.2 Gbps total bandwidth and up to 1,500 sq ft of coverage. Setup works through the Nighthawk app or WPS pairing, at a $25 to $50 price.

Fourth place follows because it matches the RE315's coverage but costs more, and its listing gives no 5 GHz speed or antenna detail. The value is in setup: an app that walks you through placement is a real benefit for anyone who has struggled with WPS.

Choose it if you already use NETGEAR gear or want guided setup. Compare the RE315 first, as it offers the same coverage for less.
products.idealFor: NETGEAR owners and anyone who wants guided setup.

products.name: TP-Link Dual Band WiFi Extender with Ethernet Port
products.verdict: A dual-band plug-in with an Ethernet port for a TV or console.
products.description:
This compact TP-Link extender is dual band across 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz, covers up to 1,200 sq ft and includes an Ethernet port. The listing says it adds up to 44% more bandwidth than an N300 single-band unit. Price is under $25.

Fifth place reflects that 1,200 sq ft is the smallest stated coverage here and the listing gives no AC speed class. Its advantage is the wired port: you can plug a TV, console or desktop into the extender and avoid Wi-Fi loss on that device.

Buy it for a bedroom entertainment setup. The caveat is that the 44% figure compares against old N300 hardware, not against modern AC units.
products.idealFor: Wired TVs and consoles in a single room.
products.skipIf: You need to cover a large home.

products.name: PEDUMMY WiFi Extender 1200Mbps
products.verdict: A 1200 Mbps dual-band unit with Ethernet and AP mode, but a coverage claim to doubt.
products.description:
PEDUMMY lists 1200 Mbps total (867 Mbps on 5 GHz plus 300 Mbps on 2.4 GHz), an Ethernet port and both extender and AP modes. It also claims coverage of up to 5,200 sq ft, more than double the AX3000's 2,400 sq ft.

It ranks last because that claim does not match its hardware class: the AX3000 has a faster radio and directional antennas and claims less. We treat the number as marketing and discount it. The AP mode is the useful extra, since it turns the unit into an access point when you have a cable to the router.

Buy it only if AP mode matters. It costs $25 to $50.
products.idealFor: Wired-backhaul setups that need AP mode.
products.skipIf: You rely on the coverage figure.

whatMatters.detail: Wi-Fi 6 handles more devices and higher speeds than Wi-Fi 5, but only if your router speaks it too. The AX3000 is Wi-Fi 6, the rest are Wi-Fi 5. Check your router's standard before paying for an AX extender, because mismatched gear runs at the lower speed.

The 5 GHz band carries most of your fast traffic, and its stated speed is the practical ceiling. The AX3000 lists 2404 Mbps and the RE315 lists 867 Mbps. Look for a 5 GHz figure on the listing, not just a combined total, because the total includes the slow band.

External adjustable antennas let you aim signal along hallways, while directional antennas with beamforming focus it on devices. Internal antennas are fixed. Check whether the listing says adjustable, high-gain or directional, and plan outlet placement halfway between the router and the dead zone.

A wired port lets a TV or console skip the wireless hop, which lowers latency and loss. The TP-Link with Ethernet and the PEDUMMY list one. Check the listing for the port, and remember that the RE315 and RE550 are not described as having one.

Coverage figures assume open space and nothing in the way. Real range falls with walls and floors, and a claim twice the size of a faster unit's is a warning. Compare the claim with the radio class, as the PEDUMMY's 5,200 sq ft against the AX3000's 2,400 sq ft.

faq.q: Will an extender work with any router?
faq.a: Yes, extenders generally work with any router, but they run at the lower of the two standards. The AX3000 on a Wi-Fi 5 router performs like an AC unit.

faq.q: What mistake do people make with extenders?
faq.a: Placing them in the dead zone. The unit must sit halfway, where it still gets a strong signal. The RE550's three adjustable antennas help you aim the signal after placement.

faq.q: Is the AX3000 worth it over the RE550?
faq.a: Only with a Wi-Fi 6 router. The AX3000 offers up to 2404 Mbps on 5 GHz against the RE550's 1.9 Gbps total, but costs several times more, so most homes should buy the RE550.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Plug it in near the router, pair it by WPS or app, then move it halfway to the dead zone. The NETGEAR EX5000 uses the Nighthawk app for guided placement.

faq.q: Does an extender slow my internet?
faq.a: It can, because it repeats the signal and shares bandwidth between its two links. Using Ethernet on the extender, as on the TP-Link with Ethernet port, avoids some of that loss.

faq.q: Is the PEDUMMY's 5,200 sq ft claim real?
faq.a: Unlikely. The AX3000 has a faster radio and directional antennas and claims 2,400 sq ft. Treat the PEDUMMY figure as marketing and plan for far less coverage.

finalTake: The TP-Link AX3000 is the best extender if you have a Wi-Fi 6 router, because it offers a 2404 Mbps 5 GHz link and directional antennas. Everyone else should buy the RE550 for mid-size homes or the RE315 for a single dead room. Treat the PEDUMMY's coverage figure with caution, and place any extender halfway between router and dead zone.
